Abstract:

Raw, or mined, coal is washed with water to remove non-combustible impurities such as rock, dirt, shale, and sulfur before it is processed for power generation in thermal power plants. The coal washery wastewater (CWW) contains complex organic contaminants, such as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), as well as inorganic contaminants. These contaminants pose a risk to the environment because they are highly persistent, toxic, and resistant to conventional treatment processes. The present study aims to develop an integrated treatment technique to effectively remediate CWW by combining advanced oxidation processes (AOPs), membrane technology, and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling. Initially, the degradation of a specific PAH, Anthracene, is investigated using AOPs like photocatalysis. The Nickel Ferrite (NiFe2O4) is examined as a visible-light-responsive photocatalyst for the degradation of Anthracene. The solvothermal method is considered to synthesize NiFe2O4. The characterization outcomes confirmed the formation of crystalline NiFe2O4 and the presence of Fe, Ni, and O. Photocatalytic degradation of Anthracene using NiFe2O4 was evaluated under visible-light irradiation by investigating the effects of catalyst dosage, pH, initial Anthracene concentration, and irradiation time. The degradation efficiency increased from 32.84% to 73.63% as the catalyst dosage increased from 1 to 5 g/L, with maximum degradation achieved within 180 min under illuminated conditions. In comparison, only 5.9% degradation was observed under dark conditions, confirming the important contribution of photocatalytic activity. Furthermore, membrane technology will be used to remove inorganic contaminants from CWW by leveraging the chemical, thermal, and mechanical stability of novel membranes. A CFD model is then developed and experimentally validated to examine membrane flow behavior, hydrodynamics, concentration distribution, and mass-transfer characteristics during filtration. Finally, experimental and numerical results will be integrated to develop a scalable treatment process capable of removing organic and inorganic contaminants from CWW. The proposed technique will provide a robust and effective strategy for remediating CWW efficiently. &nbsp
